This phenomenon produces a characteristic tail in the ejected material, with the repulsive force initially equivalent to the gravitational force but then decreasing as it moves further from the object. The initial direction of the ejections is related to the direction of the repulsive force and the path follows a parabolic trajectory under the influence of this force.

Observations of a phenomenon known as the afterglow from fast radio bursts, which follow the initial burst in about an hour, have still not resolved whether the afterglow emission is delayed or occurs concurrently with the initial burst.  By analyzing spectral data from seven sharp fast radio bursts, analysts have set the following boundaries for how quickly the afterglow must emit in order to be seen: for a narrowband model, the afterglow can only emit in the first 10 seconds if it has a frequency range of only 144 MHz, otherwise it would be seen in the first two seconds.  On the other hand, for a broader band model of 3273 MHz, the afterglow can only emit in the first two seconds if it has a peak brightness of 10^41 erg/s, otherwise it would be seen in the first 10 seconds.  These boundaries for these two models of afterglow emission set an upper limit for how long it takes for the afterglow to appear, which is essentially the time it takes for the afterglow to travel from the source to us.  Therefore, for a narrowband model of 144 MHz, the afterglow can only be delayed by no more than 10 seconds, while for a broader band model of 3273 MHz, the afterglow can only be delayed by no more than 2 seconds, which is the time it takes for the afterglow to travel from the source to us

We utilize inverse design techniques to create a high-powers stable oscillators configuration that supports high spatial and temporal modes. The development of this configuration begins with an ultra-short pulse frequency domain mode solver that employs a novel symmetry-based method to calculate electro-optic properties. Utilizing a convolution-based approach, we have enhanced the fast-axis ellipticity of the device, achieving near-Gaussian fast-axis elevation while maintaining the desired beam quality and Cauchy-like curvature in the fast-axis direction. Initially, we generated 3.3 kW of average power with a temporal coherence time of 35 fs and a fill factor of 0.35. Conversely, to produce high-power continuous wave modes, we employed inverse design to create a multi-element domain engine to direct energy toward several elements. Subsequently, we fabricated a Yb: FLINEMAN laser with 88 dB of power expansion, producing up to 220 kW of average power with a fill factor of 0.98.

The advancement of natural language processing has significantly contributed to various text generation applications but they are incapable of creating images. In contrast, computer graphics and painting are traditional forms of art, requiring visual output and often guided by guidelines. This study proposes a method for combining language models with visual controls to create image-based text, specifically incorporating guidelines related to brushstroke, color, and texture. We have developed a way to include additional guiding parameters in text input, allowing for the use of large language models that lack visual capabilities, and have created a dataset of artistic names written in a brushstroke style using neural text generation. Our approach is demonstrated through two case studies: generating brushstroke-style names for artwork and designer brands, utilizing the ArtLex dictionary. The produced texts not only convey semantic meaning but also effectively convey aesthetic visual qualities through the integration of visual controls.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in the first publicly available anonymous cryptocurrencies that leverage a form of proof of stake. The revised transaction encoding was designed to reduce computational complexity and enhance performance while maintaining the anonymity and security properties of the original Bitcoin RingCT. A comprehensive evaluation involving both theoretical and experimental analyses was employed to confirm the security and efficiency of the proposed protocol. Although faster than the original RingCT, our protocol's security was tested through various scenarios and found to be comparable to Bitcoin's RingCT.

For every detector in an ATLAS brightness scan data set, there are over 130 million individual channel readings across a 15-second interval, resulting from the large number of integrated front-end electronics channels. These integrated values represent a weighted average of photodiode light sensor readings across the entire ATLAS photodetector modules. Since individual photodetectors have distinct characteristics, the analyzed data considers only fully integrated readings, discarding partial integration results. Given the rare occurrence of fully integrated data, particularly in favor or favoring against specific beam current levels, the brightess scan analysis focuses on detecting both the presence and absence of signal. The method is capable of detecting changes in mean value and relative proportions of signal and noise across different beam current levels, yet remains ineffective in analyzing extreme low and high current levels due to incomplete integrated data. Moreover, partial ionization, a phenomenon that appears as single-channel signals not part of a photon circle, is also identified through brightness scan analysis. The method reveals that despite being relatively rare, partial ionization consistently favors high beam current levels and tends to increase in intensity as the beam current rises.

To enhance the accuracy of simulations in the physical sciences, scientists often combine data from multiple experimental or observational sources.  Currently, there are two main approaches to integrate data into existing models: a holistic strategy known as data-informed modeling, which treats multiple datasets as independent inputs; and a methodical approach, which involves combining datasets in small groups and using the results to refine models.  Due to the labor-intensive nature of this latter approach, researchers have typically preferred to analyze datasets individually, despite its efficiency.  Our study develops an automated technique that combines data-informed modeling and the methodical approach, thereby balancing the accuracy of the former with the efficiency of the latter.  This new strategy, known as collaborative data-informed modeling, uses the results of smaller dataset combinations to refine a general model, which it then applies to new, larger datasets.  Our results, demonstrated through multiple case studies in the physical sciences, show that this approach yields models of equal accuracy and lower computational cost compared to the holistic data-informed modeling strategy, even when analyzing larger datasets individually.

Our investigation into the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a lower-mass $\Upsilon(nS)$ state, accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, is the first to explore this specific type of decay. Utilizing the observed mass of $\Upsilon(10753)$, we've determined the mass of its excited partner, $m_{\Upsilon(10755)} = 10755.6 \pm 0.6 \pm 0.2$ MeV. The predicted branching ratios for this type of decay are consistent with current experimental data. The difference in masses between $\Upsilon(10753)$ and an excited $\Upsilon(nS)$ state paired with non-quark-annihilation $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles is driven by a loop process involving four particles. The predicted mass spectrum for this type of decay is provided in the search section. This work presents a novel optimization method, known as AskewSGD, inspired by range-constrained principles, to efficiently train neural networks with quantized weights. The algorithm iteratively refines the network's effectiveness on a training dataset, leveraging a diverse set of range-constrained objectives to mitigate local optima and enhance generalization. The paper provides a comprehensive examination of the algorithm's parameters and their interaction, showcasing its superiority over conventional Stochastic Gradient Descent training on low-precision neural architectures. The findings are published in a technical report, detailing empirical results and askewsgd code, available on the Hhub repository.

Over the past few decades, treatment of diseases and injuries has become increasingly more complicated, prompting robots to assist medical professionals in operative procedures by offering alternative perspectives and controlling the distribution of force to patients. In response to safety concerns and the necessity for precision, researchers have focused on the development of "soft" robots with flexible structures that adapt to fit over objects or comply when encountering obstacles, allowing them to complete tasks both internally and outside the human body. As these robots take on increasingly complex medical roles, they require more sophisticated control mechanisms that enable them to react quickly and make decisions autonomously. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of recent methods for controlling these robots in medical applications, focusing particularly on model-driven approaches that leverage mathematical representations of the robot's behavior to enhance performance, adapt to unexpected situations, and increase safety. However, reviewing the existing literature has made it clear that there are several challenges that need to be addressed before these robots can be trusted in operational medical settings, including the challenges related to maintaining an accurate understanding of the robot's behavior, integrating mathematical models with image information, and ensuring the reliable operation of the control systems.

A thorough examination is conducted on the Jacobi group (G_2(a,k)), focusing
on its action, representation, orbit, and the resulting invariant varieties.
Given that many descriptions of the Jacobi group are incomplete or missing in
existing literature, the goal of this study is to provide a comprehensive and
valid description of this group. Consequently, the paper aims to establish a
theoretical framework for calculating its character by starting with the
underlying mathematical object, rather than employing a character formula. 
Building upon this framework, the paper explores the group's homomorphisms and
use this information to derive a generalized invariant operator of the Jacobi
group (G_2(a,k)). Moreover, the study examines several special cases:
specifically, the cases when the fields have characteristic 0 or 5, as well as
in the case of the authentic Jacobi group over the real number field.

In natural language processing, fact verification involves determining the truth of a statement from a given text or using language as a source. We focus on "table-oriented" facts like "Emma has a book" when referring to a specific individual, rather than general facts. Current systems fall short in proving the validity of these types of facts, especially when considering complex situations with multiple individuals. Our research aims to address this challenge through disintegration - breaking down complex facts into simpler components by identifying key words that affect the truthfulness. By applying this method, we can effectively validate varied and complex facts. We developed a comprehensive rule set that covers various scenarios and successfully applied it to validate facts in both single and multiple-person contexts. Our unique approach was validated through human evaluation, confirming its accuracy and reliability. Furthermore, our disintegration method also exhibits significant efficiency gains, proving valuable in practical applications.

Generative adversarial networks have been applied in various fields due to their capability for creating realistic data samples. Research into GANs has primarily been focused on their ability to capture the visible properties of a dataset. Incorpororing prior knowledge into this structure can result in superior results. especially when data characteristics are difficult to determine. This leads to a hidden space in which prior knowledge is embedded. The interplay between visible and hidden spaces significantly affects the model's performance. Consequently. establishing the most effective configuration for this interplay is crucial. Using the Noisy Conditional Bit Flipping decoding algorithm in the hidden space leads to superior results when compared to alternative configurations. The GAN model incorporating NCBF is termed the Hidden Space Conditioning GAN (HSC-GAN). Recent studies have indicated that HSC-GAN outperforms previous models in terms of generating authentic samples. The potential of this model lies in its ability to incorporate diverse forms of prior knowledge. extending its successful application to various complex datasets.

In experimental signal processing, acquiring a complete dataset can be impractically costly, leading to the implementation of subsampling techniques to achieve satisfactory results. This study focuses on a specific subsampling method, utilizing phase samplers to select signals and thereby guarantee usable outputs. To this end, several researchers have proposed different phase samplers over the years. This paper aims to evaluate a novel sampler introduced in a recent study, alongside an existing high-rate sampler and two alternative solutions proposed in prior works. The results of our numerical experiments have shown that the new sampler produces comparable or, in some cases, superior outcomes, while taking less time to execute.

In the distance labeling problem, a label is assigned to each node in an undirected and connected graph with no multiple edges, such that the distance between two nodes can be determined by comparing their labels, with the optimal label size being $\Theta(n^2$. However, this optimal label size problem becomes more complex when we consider faults, as a 2-approximation algorithm for fault-resilient distance labeling gives an optimal label size of $\tilde{O}(n^{4/3})$. We propose a randomized pre-computation technique to improve fault-resilient distance labeling in connected and planar graphs with no self-loops or multiple edges. By assuming an $(\alpha,\beta)$-fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme exists, we develop an efficient algorithm that converts it into a $(\alpha+\beta+1,2)$-fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme with the same label size in expected time. We apply this technique to obtain an optimal fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme in connected and planar graphs with no self-loops or multiple edges, giving an $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ optimal label size in probability. We also derive an upper bound and a lower bound for fault-resilient distance labeling in connected and planar graphs with no self-loops or multiple edges in terms of the maximum degree $\Delta$ and the number of nodes $n$, leading to the conclusion that the range of possible values of $\epsilon$ in

We investigate the collective properties of a modified Bose-Hubbard model, incorporating features of incoherent feeders and extractable quanta, as well as the interplay between these effects. The model consists of two non-interacting groups of particles, with one experiencing loss driven by a heat bath and the other as an active source. The relationship between the particle loss and extraction is examined through their shared density matrix, and how this influences the thermal equilibrium state. The thermal equilibrium is represented by a Gibbs state, and we determine the optimal parameters to achieve a Gibbs state identical to the system's thermal equilibrium state. The study also considers a related loss mechanism, affecting only the active particles, and compares its moment and spectrum properties under two different correlation scenarios. The model exhibits unique properties such as increased non-classical properties and enhanced coherence that are a result of its underlying quantum characteristics. The essential conditions for these effects to emerge are moment or spectrum-based, and when applied to different parts of the system, various combinations of these effects are possible, influencing the quantum characteristics of the system.

We examine a key second-order elliptic equation in a $C^2$ domain, with $L^2$ constraints represented by a vector field and its associated matrix. Utilizing a H\"older continuous harmonic extension, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the equation under certain regularity conditions, with implications for the regularity of its solution. Specifically, we derive the $W^{2, p}$ regularity of the solution in the domain for any $p\in [2, \infty)$. Our approach is grounded in the generalized strong maximum principle and the existence of a suitable $W^{2, 2}$ extension.

In high-stakes areas like cybersecurity and medical diagnostics, accurately identifying outliers among a large volume of data is of paramount importance. In scenarios where data may be corrupted by an anomaly, typically referred to as an intruder, detecting such instances from a dataset to prevent contamination of subsequent data collections is essential. Although numerous techniques exist for outlier detection, this task remains challenging in partially-observed datasets, particularly in areas where anomaly detection is performed on a per-data-point basis. To address this issue, we propose the use of Gaussian Process (GP) posterior distributions as a generalized framework for analyzing the irregularities in a dataset. This comprehensive approach allows for the efficient identification of anomalies using computational operations that scale linearly with the sample size. Furthermore, this technique can also recognize patterns over irregular spatial areas, and it can be used to detect changes in real-time environments, with the sample efficiency being proportional to the change size. This method has been successfully tested using artificial and real-world datasets and has shown remarkable effectiveness.

Numerical investigations have shown that there is an equilibrium phase shift from a Bose-Einstein condensate to a Bose gas with reduced entanglement in a one-dimensional driven and trapped Bose gas with open boundaries. This phase shift occurs due to an accelerated heating process triggered by a quasi-stationary state exhibiting scar-like characteristics. The quasi-stationary state develops within the system when certain parameters are optimized. Specifically, this state emerges as a localized mode in the system's density profile. When an initial state in its ground state coherently interacts with the quasi-stationary state, it becomes aligned with the latter through a localized entanglement exchange, ultimately transitioning into the phase characterized by a Bose gas with reduced entanglement. The aggregate, in the Bose gas phase, possesses the same localized features as the quasi-stationary state, potentially enabling the production of macroscopic entanglement within the system.

Consider a modified Alexandrov problem that involves the Monge-Ampere equation in two dimensions, with specific constraints on its right-hand side. By utilizing convex geometry concepts, we demonstrate that solutions exhibit smoothness and conformal symmetry. Theoretical results derive from the study of equality cases in convex geometry. Specifically, we have found equality candidates among convex curves with distinct features, based on their placement relative to given lines. The main outcome establishes that solutions possess a C2 region in the upper half-plane, with C2 smoothness on its boundary, while also satisfying it exhibits uniform Holder continuity within the upper half-plane. The result generalized the work of A. Chang and M. Chao. Furthermore, we have shown that the C2 region can be located in the upper and lower half-plane. The approach to solving this problem involved constructing convex curves from given lines to understand equal candidate cases. The result was further explored using an example with significance in conformal geometry.

To build reliable optical clocks that operate independently and with minimal variation, a thorough technical framework is needed for assessing their performance over time. Existing theories are developed for optical clocks with consistent pulses, but the creation of such stable clocks is challenging due to fluctuations in optical signals. A new statistical model, therefore, is presented for describing optical clocks with irregular oscillations in terms of optical signal intensity over time. This model accounts for the average frequency, fluctuation patterns, and timing of optical signals using established techniques for stable systems, even when their stability is changing. The techniques for analyzing irregular fluctuations are then applied to the model, allowing for the comparison of optical clocks with stable or irregular oscillations in terms of their accuracy, response to changes, and ability to repeat previous events.

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) has driven significant progress in network flexibility, however its efficacy is hindered by the inefficiencies of traditional network management systems. This limitation will be addressed by integrating Service Function Chaining (SFC) into an energy-efficient, fog-based SDN framework, which incorporates collaborative failure recovery, fault avoidance, and efficient resource allocation mechanisms to optimize real-time networking performance. This innovative framework will achieve robustness, reliability, security, and efficiency by seamlessly integrating these features into a fully virtualized, programmable network environment. Our approach will demonstrate superior results in terms of end-to-end networking delay, energy consumption, and overall network throughput. Our extensive simulations will confirm the practical validity of this concept.

Deep neural networks have achieved tremendous success in various image-based tasks, thanks to their capacity for complex feature extraction. However, their reliance on numerical output necessitates careful selection of the loss function and associated parameter configurations to ensure accurate class manipulation. Research has shown that class separation can be controlled by adjusting the loss function in specific scenarios, raising questions about the robustness of trained models across different loss functions and parameter settings. In this study, an analysis of the outcomes of various loss functions and parameter settings is conducted, alongside an investigation into the impact of gradient manipulation to enhance class separation. The results reveal that distinct loss functions and parameter configurations lead to differences in performance and discriminability, and that a specific combination of the Focal-Cosine loss and parameters achieves the best discriminability; furthermore, a systematic analysis of gradient manipulation strategies demonstrates its effectiveness in improving model robustness and discriminability when used sparingly. The findings provide valuable insights for practitioners to select the most suitable loss function and parameter settings for a given dataset, and illustrate the importance of gradient information even in pre-training stages.

In the context of holographic quantum error correction, there's a crucial requirement for systems that can correct themselves in the radiative environment of AdS/CFT. One practical way to achieve this is by creating a type of holographic code called a reflection pair, consisting of a bulk code and its associated boundary code that can correct it. A certain class of these codes, known as power-law associations, are particularly useful and easy to work with because they're defined by their behavior in the bulk and have simple, mathematically consistent properties at the boundary. In this paper, we're introducing a type of refinement to these error-correcting codes called hyper-invariant MERAs, a version of the multi-scale entanglement renormalization framework that can represent all the different levels of these reflective pairs simultaneously. This version of MERA has the ability to capture the self-correcting properties of these codes at different scales and has been shown to have direct relationship with the properties of entanglement in the bulk space. By studying the properties of these codes in different environments, we've discovered a relationship between the properties of these codes in the bulk and at the boundary that can be described as a type of duality. Previous studies of the galactic center region's fiber population yielded results indicating the existence of uniform probability distributions for fiber bundle separation in both the horizontal and vertical planes, with each fiber considered in relation to every other fiber. Furthermore, it was observed that the average distance between fibers was roughly 0.3 parsecs. In the current research, a more detailed examination of these distributions is undertaken, focusing specifically on the statistical properties of distance between individual fibers across 16 different fields within the $\lceil l, b \rceil = 1^{\circ}$ region. By analyzing the second moment of these distributions, it was concluded that 80% of fibers are within 0.2 parsecs of each other, and that the average distance between fibers across all fields is 0.691 parsecs. While the distribution of fiber bundle separation appears uniform at first glance, close examination reveals the presence of distinct statistical outliers.

Voltage regulators, particularly automatic voltage regulators and smart switches, are crucial components in modern distribution networks for maintaining optimal voltage levels at consumer premises. However, traditional therapeutic approaches, which focus on individual transformers, often create unintended consequences, such as over-correcting for under-voltaged areas and under-correcting for over-voltaged areas. In response, researchers have introduced a conserved action approach that utilizes complex algorithms to coordinate the control of voltage regulators across multiple transformers. This paper develops a novel, decentralized technique for maintaining optimal voltage levels in a complex network with multiple voltage regulators. The method ensures that the network's energy consumption remains within predetermined limits and can adapt to changes in energy consumption patterns. In a test scenario, the proposed method demonstrated superior performance over a comparative therapeutic approach, resulting in lower total complex action potential.

We investigate a multi-armed bandit problem with specialized bandits whose performance depends on both strategy and arm interactions. Each strategy generates a sequence of discrete time periods, and a bandit's quality function varies based on these time points across different strategies. Existing analysis methods fall short in this context, as they often infer random and uniformly distributed time points, which does not accurately reflect the true conditions. By recognizing that geometric progressions offer a more accurate model for such scenarios, we can determine that the only arm strategies resulting in regular geometric progressions are optimal for generalizing to any quality function, given an unlimited number of observations. This breakthrough leads to the first efficient algorithms capable of achieving optimal geometric convergence within any time frame for various quality functions, such as noisy and non-decreasing, log-square, square, and linear functions. Our study lays the groundwork for a new theory of multi-armed bandit problems with specialized bandits and arm-dependent performance functions.

Human conversations incorporate a diverse array of discourse elements like prior discussions, emotional states, and individual viewpoints, which are all interconnected and influenced by contextual factors like tone and intention. Currently, dialogue management models that generate text are limited by a pre-defined set of responses, emotions, and perspectives, but they often fail to effectively incorporate contextual information, resulting in a fragmented and non-coherent dialogue. In contrast, a well-structured approach to discourse is able to successfully draw upon various sources to create a nuanced and human-like text production outcome. Drawing from the advantages of both template-based and generative methods, we present the LEATHER framework for Acquiring to Produce Human-like Text in Dialogue, which organizes discourse elements into distinct categories that are interrelated by contextual factors like conversational history, emotional states, and perspectives. Additionally, LEATHER incorporates a unified language model that enables the integration of these disparate elements into a coherent text, even when the discourse elements are unclear or unavailable. In our study, we analyzed the effects of varying the scale and specificity of the input elements on text production and discovered that larger models and more precise elements lead to improved text production. Notably, our results indicate that this productive effect is particularly evident in scenarios where the discourse elements are ambiguous, thus highlighting the importance of a comprehensive framework in producing a natural and engaging dialogue.

Following the breakthroughs in the 1990s, when lattice QCD began successfully testing many previously untested observables in excess of unitarity, the field made considerable progress over the past two decades. Key breakthroughs included advancements in the treatment of dynamic fermions, the application of molecular dynamics and partial invariance under continuous symmetries, the development of cluster algorithms for complex actions, the improvement of simulations at small quark masses through the application of monomers and spin matrices, and the integration of the center, a crucial component of QCD, into the aforementioned methods. Consequently, the computational demands of simulations have reached an unprecedented level of sophistication. This text provides an introduction to the state of the art in lattice QCD for non-zero temperature and density. The author's contributions to this state of the art are presented in the respective chapters on lattice measurements of the QCD gauge phase diagram.

As the rapid advancement of renewable energy captures public's attention, the cost reduction driven by technological improvement will likely gain more emphasis from a sustainability perspective. Predictive modeling has emerged as a crucial factor in the development of this industry, enabling businesses to make informed investment and operation decisions. For the offshore wind energy sector, which is witnessing an exceptionally high growth rate, the accuracy of stress predictions directly influences core aspects like structural integrity, annual energy production, and installation complexity. In this study, a probabilistic modeling framework that seamlessly integrates linked Gaussian Processes is applied to simulate the stresses on offshore wind turbines, which simulates the intercorrelation between various loads impacting these structures. The results of our model have demonstrated promising potential, exhibiting mean squared errors lower than predicted load predictions and demonstrating increased correlation resolution between stress types for the specific offshore wind turbine in our analysis, the Siemens SWT-3.6-77.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with significant earthquakes occurring relatively frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis response. In this study, we investigate the usefulness of social media listening in this context. We employed data collection techniques and an BERT-based classification model for detecting crisis-related tweets over a specific timeframe. We focused on an earthquake in Izmir that occurred on July 20, 2022, and collected 32,114 relevant tweets for further analysis. Our results demonstrate that the developed model can filter relevant content from a large social media dataset in a crisis situation, and that tweet content exceeding 180 characters does not adversely affect the model's performance. We visually present aggregated data on tweet counts, and break down the derived labels into distinct categories, while also analyzing the most frequent related words in each category. We utilize the generated labels to create visualizations of users who actively contributed to the discourse, and those who engaged more than 5 times in the discussion within an hour of the earthquake. Additionally, our analysis of engagement patterns in online content streams shows that users who discussed the earthquake in detail (such as earthquake parameters) in a concise manner were relatively few in number. We present two different types of embeddings: words and users, and apply clustering analysis to the word embeddings, revealing distinct categories such as "earthquake-related" and "quake aftermath" labels. We obtain similar labels when applying clustering to the user embeddings. We utilize the generated labels to create an interactive visualization of the derived concept map

A standardized way of characterizing finite groups was developed by Miller and Gurevich in 2004 to effectively identify solvable groups by utilizing a specialized two-group quotient. In this study, we extend the R∞ characteristic to finite nilpotent groups and investigate its applicability to quotients of the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group. We also establish a method to determine all nilpotent groups of a specific type that can be found as quotients of the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group.

A novel spatiotemporal deconvolution method is created for data obtained through time-resolved observations, specifically designed for tracking surface reaction progress with high depth resolution using techniques like Photoemission Electron Yield (PEY). This approach leverages a forward-kinetics model, combining first principle and empirical descriptions, to simulate reaction progress. A stabilization technique is employed to prevent overfitting by constraining model components, followed by regularizing the optimization problem using a Tikhonov method. As a result, highly reliable and reproducible descriptions of reaction progression can be achieved, even in later stages. This approach offers robustness and is particularly suitable for observing surface reactions that involve gas-surface interactions.

Automated driving systems rely heavily on natural image datasets to learn policy decisions.
Despite existing datasets being effective for policy acquisition, they fall short of replicating the complexity of real-world scenarios when it comes to perception tasks.
A notable limitation of these datasets is their lack of connection to the surrounding environment, as they are typically generated through simulation. 
Our approach addresses this gap with a novel driving dataset called SceNDD, which is specifically designed for naturalistic driving applications.
This dataset is distinguished by its extensive contextual information, comprising real-world scenes captured from multiple angles, ranging from ultra-wide to telephoto focal lengths.
Our goal in creating SceNDD is to provide a unique resource for machine learning algorithms focused on naturalistic driving tasks to learn from.
The dataset can be accessed online at https://sites.google.com/view/sendd.

In this research, the concept of Reflected Entropy in conformal field models with a boundary/interface present is introduced and computed for specific instances. Its relationship with previous findings on boundary reflection and partition functions within this context is explored, particularly regarding the partition function for the boundary free field.

A reliable and efficient channel estimation scheme is proposed for a range of users assisted by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) in an OFDM-based system. To enhance performance, the proposed method incorporates an optimal data-driven training matrix, an optimized WLS estimation approach, and a sophisticated iterative refinement strategy. Firstly, an optimal TT matrix is designed through an SDP optimization, in conjunction with a low-rank RIS channel approximation, to effectively estimate the RIS phase-shift matrix. Next, an optimized WLS approach is used in conjunction with the proposed TT matrix to estimate the combined channel matrix. Finally, an iterative refinement strategy is employed to rectify estimation errors using conventional LS methods. The results indicate that the proposed scheme outperforms existing models, including a hybrid RIS-SS/OFDM channel estimation method, in terms of estimation accuracy, especially when training symbols are insufficient or system hardware malfunctions occur.

We examine the connection between energy fluctuations of a system subjected to external non-invasive testing and its inherent properties. Our findings indicate that the anomalous behavior of the system under such testing is characterized by specific values of its size and the exponent of its energy distribution. These outcomes are relevant in the context of statistical analysis of complex systems, particularly those involving financial markets.

An important investigation has been carried out regarding the deformations of G2-instantons. It is first established that deformations of G2-instantons on a nearly G2 manifold are inherently one-connected. The study goes on to demonstrate that their deformations come in a single, unified form. The impact of self-intersection of the associated 7-dimensional sphere has been found to play a decisive role in the degeneration of deformations. The researchers also identified the specific conditions under which vector deformations exist for G2-instantons. The outcomes of this investigation have been applied to the specific case of a solitons presence in Euclidean spaces.

With the rapid spread of the novel Coronavirus in early 2020, countries with large populations like Brazil were faced with overwhelming hospital admissions, straining public health services. To mitigate this, national authorities introduced contact tracing COVID-19 applications to enforce social distancing policies, while ensuring healthcare staff could focus on patient assessment and treatment. Although these measures were highly effective in reducing infections, they also raised significant data protection concerns and risks of data misuse. In this context, our investigation aims to examine the confidentiality of the Coronavirus-SUS COVID19 application, widely used in Brazil, by evaluating its compliance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation. Notably, the Coronavirus-SUS COVID19 system is the primary data collection tool for epidemiological monitoring, with over 14 million user registrations. Given its pivotal role in public health, our research not only scrutinizes the system's individual modules, but also explores its broader implications on public health and democracy, with a view to identifying best practices for similar COVID-19 apps. While the Coronavirus-SUS COVID19 was developed in accordance with Brazilian Law 13,449/2017, our analysis reveals several concerns regarding the processing of public health user data, with our key contributions including the development of a formal context and a formal security policy, as well as the application of the Bogdanov-Berger inequality to evaluate the security of the system using disclosed data. Although the results do not necessarily imply a security breach, they do highlight significant confidentiality risks

Researchers have been exploring the potential of combining quantum computing with artificial neural networks. This could lead to significant advancements in both quantum and deep learning fields. In this study, we examine the concept of quantum data in neural networks. We begin by categorizing quantum data in relation to classical data and discuss its fundamental properties. Additionally, we compare quantum data with encrypted classical data. We then discuss how to generate quantum data and represent it in a standard format. Furthermore, we establish a mathematical framework for differentiating through quantum data and exploring its characteristics in both discrete and continuous contexts. Finally, we outline future research pathways focused on developing and optimizing quantum data for neural networks.

This research introduces a tool for automatically generating C code that is provably correct in ACL2 based on the existing superficial embedding of C in ACL2. Developed on the principles of proof-by-reification, the toy tool constructs C code refinements for ACL2 functions with embedded C elements and proves their correctness through reifications of ACL2 theorems. Since the embedded C code in ACL2 is free of side effects, the generated C code's interactive behavior can be accurately represented. The tool's effectiveness was demonstrated through the successful development of a ACL2 model of a robotic arm and the creation of a C controller for it. A major advantage of this research is the ability to break down complex multi-paradigm proofs into simpler components, thereby facilitating the creation of multi-paradigm proof strategies.

Investigations into the high-energy resonance behavior of three key systems involving
the interaction of the J$\psi$ and $\Sigma_c$ meson with the $\rho$ and $\omega$ vector meson
reveal significant and unanticipated fluctuations in resonance cross sections and coupling
constants, which may influence the interpretation of experimental results. We demonstrate
how these resonance variations could be associated with a long-deleted planet in the Iochroma system.

Building upon Ramanujan's work on odd zeta values, we establish a formula using Hurwitz zeta functions, thereby providing a precise answer to a question posed by Henryk Fuks. Additionally, we derive an integral representation of these functions, analogous to a result from Eisenstein's research. Our proof relies on the use of the Gauss sum and a specific identity related to parity, which is then extended to include more general cases involving the product of zetas. This allows us to create a sequence of terms that ultimately leads to a combinatorial interpretation of the Euler Gamma function. Finally, we leverage the theory of periodicity to develop an expression for calculating zeta functions by multiplying an even zeta function by a factor accounting for periodicity.

We establish in this research that the elliptic cohomology theory $E_{t_0}(R)$, as developed in elliptic cohomology theory, is isomorphic to the equivariant version $E_{t_0}(R)\{\tau\}$ of the theory $E_{t_0}(R)$ when considering the action of the group $\mathbb{C}^*\times\mathbb{C}^*$ on the projective space $\mathbb{P}(V)$ for a given vector space $V$. This is achieved by extending the Ossa-Sanchez-Valenzuela construction, as first presented in 1990, to create a $G$-equivariant theory for the action of the group $G=\mathbb{C}^*\times\mathbb{C}^*$ on $\mathbb{P}(V)$. This result also demonstrates that the Ossa-Sanchez-Valenzuela construction can be seen as a particular instance of a more general scenario.

We employ algebraic topological techniques to create a machine-learnable representation of spaces, which we apply to the creation of optimized Hamiltonians in quantum simulation. To investigate the properties of real materials, we develop combinatorial topological models based on experimental data and use the Serre-Serre spectral sequence to compute the homology of these representations. These results enable us to identify the homology of spaces as a feasible learning objective, and we demonstrate its practical application through the prediction of phase transitions in the two-dimensional quantum magnetic material, the Kagome lattice. To facilitate research, we maintain an open-source repository of tools, datasets, and results at https://github.com/Groupy-ML/Groupy-ML.

This paper investigates the $J/\psi$ production angular distributions in $J/\psi + \eta_c(\rightarrow J/\psi \gamma_g)$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}(\rightarrow J/\psi \gamma_8)$ with leading and next-to-leading order QCD calculations, where the latter includes eight-color contributions. These measurements aim to examine the theoretical and experimental predictions made in an earlier study (arXiv:2102.04213) that analyzed $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{expt}}(t)$ components. Unlike Charmonium Systems in the Energy Range program, which evaluates t-channel predictions, this investigation looks at cross-sections in $q\bar{q} \rightarrow J/\psi + \eta_c(\chi_{cJ})$ with $t \approx -1 \,\mathrm{GeV}^2$ for $t$-channel dominance. Moreover, this study critically assesses the potential impact of next-to-leading order QCD calculations on predicted angular distributions in $J/\psi$ for $\chi_{cJ}$ and $\eta_c$ and identifies which $J/\psi$ production and annihilation processes dominate $J/\psi$ production. These results also reveal that leading and next-to-leading order QCD calculations produce indistinguishable distributions in $t$, while examining predicted and experimental $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{expt}}(t)$ components demonstrates dominance by $|t|

An evaluation of Signal was conducted involving 17 users, including 6 who used the app frequently and 11 who only used it sporadically. The research involved asking participants a series of questions about protecting their devices with Signal and PINs. The results showed users who frequently used Signal had a good understanding of how the app protects information on their devices, but those who used it less frequently had a good grasp of the general concept of PINs but not much insight into Signal's specific features. The researchers suggest that additional features and functionalities can make a service more complex and harder for users to understand.

We present a novel, high-performance algorithm for calculating the integral of a function over the unit sphere in 3D, weighted by the solar irradiance function, which varies based on solar latitude and altitude. This algorithm is tailored for efficient use on compute devices featuring multiple processing capabilities. It is adapted from pre-existing formulations that calculate solar energy input into complex geometries, and is now optimized for direct application to integrands without the need for intermediate calculations. A recently developed open-source library provides the multi-processor implementation for numerical methods, and our research includes an in-depth comparison of numerical methods for solar energy calculations. We also demonstrate a critical error reduction in the solar energy formula, and propose the development of spherical quadrature rules with built-in solar irradiance weighting for use in any 3D integration task, and show how these new rules compare to conventional quadrature methods in a range of applications.

The curvature formed by the second derivative of a function essentially represents how the objective function changes when the parameters change. In the case of optimizing machine learning models, this usually involves taking the second derivative of the loss function with respect to the model's parameters. However, this task is often computationally expensive because it requires a large entry count proportional to the square of the number of parameters in the model. In this study, we explore a more efficient approach called the ViViT method, which uses a theoretical low-dimensional structure associated with the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian to minimize computational costs. Our method can now optimize complex machine learning models much faster, thanks to our research that establishes a more direct link between the ViViT entry count and the number of parameters in the model. Our experiments show that the ViViT method outperforms other methods by achieving better accuracy and faster execution times in practical applications, such as training neural networks and solving general non-convex optimization problems in the fields of reinforcement learning and adversarial learning. Our implementation of the ViViT method is available online for free on our GitHub repository.

Many languages that exhibit distinct grammatical gender utilize noun categories to determine article and pronoun forms, leading to a fundamental relationship between gender and word identity within these languages. Conversely, languages without distinct grammatical gender often prioritize semantic cues when identifying gender in noun representations. Conversely, languages without distinct grammatical gender often prioritize semantic cues when identifying gender in noun representations. Studies have demonstrated the integration of grammatical gender into noun representations, specifically in languages with distinct categories, however, have not fully explored its effects on these representations. This paper investigates how grammatical gender influences noun representation through two representations, one for languages with distinct categories and another for languages without, by manipulating the weight assigned to gender in each model. It then analyzes and compares the performance of each model across all languages, as well as in groups of languages with and without distinct categories, specifically highlighting how grammatical gender impacts noun representations in each case.

In our investigation, we explore the concept of charmability and rigidity in the context of finite-cow Belyĭ objects. Building on the foundation laid by Chudnovsky and Zograf in 1984 and 1985 for modular forms, our study utilizes the services of Gelfand-Patel-Shlatts for its theoretical underpinning. A significant finding demonstrates that the mod $2$ complex multiplication group is a pro-$2$ rigid group characterized by its charmable subgroups being confined to the central isomorphic image of the group of integers multiple $2$ within the group, thus solving a problem initially posed by Zograf in 1985.

Estimating the class-specific position of an object in an image, known as class-level object position estimation, involves both object detection and localization without any prior knowledge of the object's presence. Since object detection and localization are related but distinct tasks, we can approach this problem by combining a detection model with a localized feature extraction method adapted from single-stage detection frameworks. As a further innovation, we suggest modifying the classification head to encoders that produce embedded representations for each class, allowing us to tackle zero-shot and hidden-object scenarios. Our proposed framework excels in comparison to baseline models, boasting a high ranking of 6th on the APE dataset benchmark for zero-shot object position estimation.

Traffic volume forecasting serves multiple purposes, such as informing urban planners and reducing congestion costs. Yet, predicting traffic for an entire city's numerous intersections is a substantial challenge due to its scale. Instead of tackling this difficulty head-on, we introduce a innovative technique called similarity-based attribute extraction for sparse traffic forecasting. This framework comprises two parts: the similarity-computation module and the attribute-extraction module. The former identifies patterns in traffic data by calculating the traffic-index time series for each location, then uses cosine similarity to group areas with similar patterns together. The latter uses machine learning and optimization techniques to analyze the time series and extract relevant features from each group. Given the scarcity of data, we employ supervised feature learning to allow our system to automatically identify the most useful features for forecasting purposes. Evaluating our approach on real-world data reveals that our feature-extraction capabilities are indeed comparable to those of a traffic expert, and our system significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in traffic forecasting.

This work presents VACA, a variational graph autoencoder framework designed to model complex relationships between multiple variables and counterfactive scenarios, particularly suitable for causal inference tasks where manipulations are in question. The development of an efficient, scalable, and intuitive variational model on a graph structure is seen as a significant contribution by the authors. Notably, VACA achieves several advancements: it surpasses state-of-the-art performance in synthetic and real-world datasets; it provides a computationally efficient method for policy optimization; and it enables the estimation of causal effects and counterfactual outcomes with enhanced interpretability and calibrability using variational inference and posterior matching techniques. The source code for the VACA model is publicly available at the repository link provided.

The future generation radio telescopes, like the Square Kilometer Array, heavily rely on software radio and vision-based technologies to optimize their operational efficiency and uncover a vast array of scientific potentials. Building upon this concept, the Research Electronics Laboratory's REALtime Transient Capture backend technology enables the real-time processing of vast AD converter data streams with cutting-edge software radio capabilities, incorporating Automated Radio Wave Intensity Extraction and other powerful features. Effective data reduction techniques are essential for managing the enormous data volumes generated by cutting-edge radio telescopes, and REALtime is at the forefront of this endeavor, combining data reduction and transmission capabilities within a single, high-density 10T board. The Irish LOFAR Facility is currently put to a test as the first site to implement REALtime, and we will discuss the outcomes of our recent joint observational efforts involving REALtime and the LOFAR Wide Field SNR instrument.

Artificial intelligence has significantly accelerated the development of metamaterials by generating infinite new structures with desired performance, thereby surpassing conventional design limitations. Nevertheless, the intricate relationship between structure and function within these complex systems often hinders their practical application and thorough comprehension. Metamaterials containing many interacting elements challenge the use of conventional machine learning methods due to the enormous amount of data required to simulate their behavior. Our team has overcome this limitation in metasemiconductors by creating highly scalable neural networks, which effectively predict the eigenstates of these complex systems. Our research demonstrates a substantial increase in artificial intelligence-driven metasemiconductor device performance through systematic device optimization. Our study also showcases an unparalleled capability to analyze artificial intelligence-driven metasemiconductors using quantum physics principles, highlighting a more comprehensive understanding of these systems than previously possible.

The primary goal of this research is to design an effective method for forecasting the gross income of films based on their trailereffects, including how the audience reacts. By combining our innovative approach with a range of previously established features, our experiments utilizing real-world data reveal that it surpasses existing techniques in accuracy. Furthermore, a comprehensive dataset containing over 1100 film reviews and 550 trailer segments has been developed specifically for this purpose. This dataset marks a significant advancement over earlier iterations, which were limited to just 16 trailers. In addition, our analysis reveals that well-established metrics such as AUC and RMSE only reveal part of the picture when evaluating how effectively a model anticipates a film's success. Therefore, our work also involves an innovative bias measurement technique that could prove valuable for future research in this field.

This study focuses on understanding the role of auxiliary frequency regulation in grid voltage stability. With the rise of photovoltaic systems in power grids, voltage problems often arise, particularly in low voltage parts of the network. To mitigate these issues, auxiliary frequency regulation systems are installed, but they can also contribute to voltage stability problems by interacting with power plants control loops. This paper examines the behavior of a grid with solar power systems, considering both passive and active power control loops, as well as auxiliary frequency regulation. A two-minute control loop is modeled at the solar park level, using the CI-D method to identify the dynamic model's parameters. To assess the effect of different control strategies on voltage stability, the authors used the NF-PTSS method to analyze the non-linear behavior of the system. A case study on a distribution network demonstrates the ability of the NF-PTSS method to predict voltage instability and provide insights for network operators to prevent overcompensation by auxiliary frequency regulation systems.

This article focuses on cyberphysical networks comprising intelligent units, where each unit employs cognitive strategies to contribute to network operations. It analyzes the mathematical structure of network information by categorizing its components into localized, conditional, and global aspects. The latter two are particularly significant in cyberphysical applications. The paper also examines how cognitive decisions are influenced by these two information types. The importance of contextual dependency in cyberphysical networks is further emphasized by examining the effects of correlated and heterogenous local information on system units. The paper's conclusions include the outcomes of combining randomized policies, the importance of contextual dependency in cyberphysical systems, and the challenges and potential benefits that arise when incorporating cognitive capabilities into cyberphysical networks.

This study employs a novel Monte-Carlo method to analyze the interaction between non-thermal, polarized electron clouds and non-thermal, non-polarized photon clouds in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole. Our model generates a continuum of diffuse synchrotron radiation throughout the optical to X-ray spectrum, as well as a possible surplus of UV excess and polarized X-ray excess radiation, which is attributed to inverse Compton scattering. The simulated data suggests that this effect could produce a significant increase in the X-ray excess, a distinction from pure blazar models, as previously researched. The simulated data also indicates that this effect could result in the detection of H-alpha to He-II polarization at higher redshifts or lower values, lower polarization percentages in the near infrared to optical range (10% to 2%), and a possible decrease or elimination of polarized radiation in the X-ray to soft gamma-ray range, as observed in some blazar spectra. The non-detection of polarized radiation in the X-ray to soft gamma-ray range in certain blazar sources, such as PKC 1258+543, 3C 279, and others, can be attributed to various factors such as reversal of polarization direction deposition, polarization dilution, absorption, and scattering. The simulated data also suggests that this effect could result in the deposition of polarized radiation in the near infrared to optical range, as observed in some blazar sources, such as PG 1244+166

This research investigates how to extend analytic functions across complex domains in a way that forms a shape preserving parameterization. We've found that for any complex region with a smooth boundary, and a conformal mapping to the unit disk, we can create a parameterization of this region using classical Pommret invariants. Additionally, we've demonstrated that these invariants can be efficiently computed using the current state of the art algorithms for conformal geometry. As practical applications of our method, we've successfully generated highly detailed and visually appealing results for 3D extension problems that previous approaches had struggled with.

We explore the virtual detection of pure states with specific symmetrical characteristics. The process involves a controllable system in a specific state that interacts with an unknown target state, resulting in no measurable output. The system's configuration is then altered to make the system target-state-ready through a sequence of controllable interactions with the target, without physically observing it. The research focuses on optimal virtual detection strategies for various key states, including Bell, GHZ, Dicke, and Werner states, with a comprehensive analysis of experimental limitations in terms of error rates and necessary interaction cycles. The study also identifies the optimal virtual detection approach for an unknown target state, demonstrating unique cycle-dependent characteristics. Notably, our findings indicate that virtual detection has minimal errors and necessitates a minimal number of interactions, which significantly correlates with the target state's symmetry properties. Additionally, our analysis highlights how detection errors and required interaction cycles vary based on specific state characteristics and scales with certain parameters.

We've discovered that baryons originate from a specific process in the quantum version of the vacuum, resulting from the breakdown of a specific type of quantum string. This string has distinct characteristics when viewed from different angles due to its complexity. The breakdown of the string into distinct parts occurs at points that aren't connected in a continuous manner. The resulting states of baryons are governed by a specific set of rules that determine their mass and other properties. We've confirmed that the rules governing baryon mass are consistent across different states. The resulting distribution of baryon mass is influenced by a specific factor that reflects the complexity of the underlying quantum system. The rules governing baryon composition are consistent with existing data and predict certain characteristics of baryon flavor.

The way seismic waves travel through the sun's interior depends on its rotation rate and temperature. Studies using the sun's interior as a rotating sphere have revealed an irregular pattern of speed variations, which some attribute to a faster rotation at the sun's equator than at its poles. However, the cause behind this phenomenon is still unclear. One theory suggests that differences in the movement of the sun's fluid inside its core and outer layers may produce different speed variations in the seismic waves within those respective regions. To investigate this, the travel times of seismic waves recorded by SOHO/BBSO in 2001 were analyzed separately from those collected before and after a sunspot activity period. The data showed that the sun's core contributes to the observed faster travel times during active periods but the sun's outer layers show a opposing effect, thus suggesting a more complex understanding is needed than just the sun's rotation rate to explain the seismic wave behavior, particularly regarding the faster travel times during active periods.

High-redshift sources emit their gravitational waves at extremely dim levels, pinning hopes on discovering a new method of detection at the level of millisecond precision. Our investigation focuses on a previously unanalyzed theory link - the interaction between magnetic fields and cosmic strings - which predicts the generation of primordial magnetic fields through the formation of magnetic bubbles during phase transitions. These magnetic fields' effects on space-time are analyzed over a wide range of scales associated with the scales of domain formation, which translates to gravitational wave frequencies. Our findings indicate that the earliest sources of gravitational waves are likely powered not by the fields themselves, but rather by the interaction with astrophysical objects like pulsars and black holes, which produce an additional timing irregularity in the Pulsar Timing Array. Our data-driven estimates reveal that the signals from the initial magneto-gravitational sources are expected to be weaker than those of PBHs and magnetic field sources linked to the formation of large-scale cosmic structures. Our investigation considers the impact of magnetic bubbles in the radiation, IntElectron, and neutrino eras with an emphasis on the ME case - this has significant implications for the Pulsar Timing Array, which might detect new sources of gravitational waves within the PTA band with future advancements.

Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest in the research community due to its varied potential uses. A significant feature of commercial plenoptic cameras, the arrangement of focal plane images, enables the reproduction of 3D objects by adapting the perspective of a light source. Nonetheless, the substantial dimensionality of light field images poses a major obstacle to their practical application, mainly because of the difficulties associated with their storage and image processing. To overcome these limitations, our study introduces an innovative model for disparity-aware light field image compression. The model in question is trained in an entirely automatic manner, simply by providing initial guidance in terms of object displacement across focal planes. The results of our experiments confirm the superiority of our proposed model when compared to the best existing solutions in the field.

A key challenge in Cross-Language Information Retrieval (CLIR) stems from the difficulty of finding equivalent documents across different languages. Multiple CLIR approaches have been explored to tackle this problem, with some frameworks focusing on interactive models requiring user input, and others favoring non-interactive models relying on pre-compiled tools. This research delves into a comparative analysis of these two CLIR methods and proposes a novel hybrid technique that combines their benefits. Our evaluation involves conducting experiments on different CLIR tasks, using various language pairs and a unified dataset. The outcome of these studies indicates that a hybrid approach incorporating elements from both frameworks yields superior performance and efficient query processing compared to standalone interactive or non-interactive methods. Our findings contribute valuable insights to the CLIR community, offering a successful combination of and benefits to support CLIR solution development and evaluation.

Uganda's 2016 General Housing and Population Census revealed that nearly 90% of its people reside in urban areas with very high population density, making it an ideal setting for small-area estimation. However, the increased focus on global health in urban settings requires accurate estimates at a more detailed sub-city level, necessitating a novel statistical challenge. We investigated the performance of renowned design- and model-focused small-area estimation methods using real-world data. Our analysis concentrated on the individual models' capabilities to produce reliable predictions and rankings of estimators. We also explored the impact of sample design on small-area estimation. Our findings suggest that the Relative Empirical Bayes and Model-Based methods produce the most reliable predictions and rankings. Our research showcases the small-area estimation methods' utility and highlights the need to select an appropriate sample design.

We've developed a novel technique for implementing the Kelly wagering strategy within a quantum environment using continuous variables. By utilizing a controlled phase modulator in an optical interferometer, we show that the natural fluctuations inherent to sequential betting can be generated through quantum fluctuations. This approach enables us to create a single optical pulse at the end of the evolution, which encompasses a value determined by a stochastic process and characterized by a mean calculated by a quantum operator and a variance dictated by the secondary moment-generating function's coefficient. Moreover, having optimized the betting fractions, the developed operator calculates the optimal stochastic process, which exhibits linear growth in its mean and zero variance. This method allows for its probabilities' distribution to be controlled via the control variable, alongside its amplitude and frequency.

The recently created two-dimensional semiconductor, MA$_2$Z$_4$ (M = Mo, W, Ti; A = Si, Ge), with its versatile properties, shows great potential in advanced electronics and quantum information devices. Using ab initio calculations, the influence of exchange interaction on the alignment of the quasiparticle energy levels is found to be significant across different stackings of the structure. Nevertheless, the exchange interaction has a minimal effect on the properties of the excitons, independent of the stacking sequence. By identifying the inherent characteristics of the exchange interaction, it becomes possible to utilize ab initio calculations to analyze the excitonic properties without the complexity of stack-dependent excitonic binding energies. The independence of the excitons from stacking sequences makes the creation of large, homogeneous MA$_2$Z$_4$ monolayers feasible, utilizing a range of synthesis techniques available today. The excitonic binding energy is estimated to be around 100 millielectronvolts, suggesting the potential for a weakly bound exciton, akin to that found in cupper selenide. The inherent excitonic characteristics, combined the inherent excitonic binding energy, presents numerous opportunities for the investigation and manipulation of the regulatory electronic properties on a ultra-strong magnetic field of MA$_2$Z$_4$ and the regulation of the electronic properties by the excitons.

This research investigates the occurrence of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ event, which is a rare phenomenon detectable within the LHCb's scope, and determines that its detection potential at the experiment is substantial. Specifically, we anticipate observing $6.67 \times 10^{-6} \pm (4.73 \pm 0.99)$ occurrences per $p^+ p^-$ collision. The listed uncertainties stem from standard muon identification methods and methods enhanced by a global fit to various lepton decays, respectively. The $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ event might be exploited in examining the existence of lepto-gluonic couplings, which is a capability unique to the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ event among those listed in our study.

The process of planet formation remains one of the greatest enigmas in astronomy, and particularly puzzling is the early development of giant planets within the surroundings of the first stars. In order to investigate the initial steps in this process, we utilized the stellarator code to simulate how planets form, using idealized models based on perfectly circular initial conditions. Our simulations, which assumed uniform mass loss from the planetary material, revealed that following the formation of a protoplanet, a new disk begins to take shape around it. This disk, which is called a circumplanetary disk, is characterized by unique rotational properties. Furthermore, our simulations showed that the presence of this disk serves to hinder further mass accumulation by the protoplanet. In our idealized models, we discovered that the mass of the protoplanet is confined to a relatively narrow range, and this phenomenon tends to persist in subsequent stages of the planet's development. In order to investigate the long-term stability of the circumplanetary disks, we utilized models based on more realistic initial conditions, which accounted for rotating and expanding star clouds. Our findings suggest that the rupture of prestellar planetary nuclei is a common occurrence in first star systems, and the circumplanetary disks surrounding these nuclei have relatively short lifetimes of a few million years. Consequently, planets are likely to encounter a disruption of their surrounding material a relatively short period after their initial formation, and this environment could play a significant role in shaping their development.

When electromagnetic signals from space travel through the atmosphere, their intensity is weakened due to various interactions. In order to minimize the impact of scattering on observations from ground-based observatories, astronomers often rely on predicting the levels of scattering. In a recent study, our team obtained direct measurements of how much different wavelengths are affected by scattering. By analyzing these effects, we were able to compare them to existing models of scattering, which revealed some discrepancies. In particular, our research emphasizes the significance of considering the variability of scattering factors across different wavelengths, giving proper weight to their uncertainties.

This paper addresses the problem of simultaneously modeling multiple terms within
a temporal sequence and identifying the infrequent occurrences in each term.
By employing a prior based on a low-rank Gaussian mixture model in the Bayesian context,
our approach can efficiently learn the underlying factors and detect less frequent
events, even with large data sets. However, existing computational and storage
requirements for full Bayesian inference are prohibitively high. Therefore, we
develop a novel variational approximation and show that a simplified posterior
derived from the average structure of mixed Gaussian distributions closely
resembles performance of the more complex posterior. Additionally, we derive
a simplified expression for the posterior via the variational approximation.
The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on simulated
data and diverse real-world time series data in neuroscience, finance, and weather.

This note begins by proving a key result on the pontrigain duality in the context of continuous abelian groups, leveraging the framework of continuous topology. It then explores an example illustrating the effect of continuous dimension on the pontrigain duality. Furthermore, this example serves to clarify the conceptual framework of continuous reasoning within the framework of continuous logic, particularly with respect to the principle of reiterable application.

The increasingly widespread use of machine learning across various social spheres has raised serious ethical concerns regarding justice and privacy. In an effort to address these issues, researchers have developed two key approaches: utilizing fair algorithms and safeguarding data confidentiality through differential privacy. However, widespread implementation of machine learning has been hindered by the need to balance data protection with intellectual property and intellectual justice. There are also significant obstacles to data sharing, including the risk of data exposure, among other privacy breaches. We propose a novel framework for federated learning that simultaneously tackles the challenges of fairness and differential privacy. Utilizing the theory of multi-objective optimization, our approach allocates the effects of gradient scaling in federated learning to serve both utility and differential privacy objectives. By applying our method to the fair federated learning problem in deep networks, we develop an algorithm that automatically adjusts the learning process. Experimental results demonstrate the ability of our method to effectively fair, and keep the results differentially private, often without compromising utility, as exemplified by accurate federated learning on skewed datasets, such as CIFAR-10, 20-Newletters, and EMNIST. Furthermore, our approach significantly improves upon existing methods that concurrently address fairness and differential privacy.

We present a supersymmetric extension of the standard model, featuring a novel $U(1)_X$ model, which introduces a dark sector consisting of a right-handed neutrino with a Majorana mass, capable of providing the universe's dark energy. In this model, light Higgs boson masses and a $Z'$ boson at the TeV scale are both feasible under a single supersymmetric $U(1)_X$ gauge group, which includes the standard model's $SU(2) \times U(1)$. We have thoroughly examined the model's supersymmetric spectrum and the phenomenology of its components, particularly focusing on the $H\bar{H}$ production, $CP$-even Higgs boson decays into $b\bar{b}$, $WZ$ and $Z$-$Z'$ systems, and the $h$-associated production with $Z'$ or additional neutralinos. Furthermore, this model's $CP$-odd Higgs boson, mixing exclusively with the standard model's $H$, is predicted to be observable at 300 GeV, with a detection prospect of up to 100 events at the HL-LHC with 300 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected. The model's signature for producing $h$ alongside $Z'$ or neutralinos will be within the reach of future HL-LHC and ILC experiments, with a detection prospect of up to 100 events at the ILC with

To improve the efficiency of a wireless network assisted by an IRS that also facilitates energy transfer, we aim to optimize the energy harvesting rate. A major obstacle is interference caused by a nearby active user, which hinders IRS performance. To resolve this issue, we suggest combining IRS with a wireless power transfer user and a passive energy harvesting user to maximize the energy harvesting rate. To achieve this, we develop a data-driven method for adjusting IRS reflection vectors. First, we create a database of optimal IRS settings for various network configurations without a disruptive user, using a machine learning approach. Next, we propose a method for modeling the impact of the disruptive user's data on the IRS assisted by a trained database. Finally, we use an iterative algorithm to adjust the IRS reflection vectors, minimizing interference from the disruptive user, resulting in enhanced energy harvesting capacity. Our results show that this method significantly outperforms a benchmark heuristic, yielding a higher normalized sum-power harvesting rate.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Tl and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the observed half-life of 52(2) ms, is in line with theoretical expectations for the initial beta decay of Mercury isotopes. The results indicate that the 186Hg(1/2- state possesses the highest initial beta strength, corresponding to a 43.1(8.1) ns isomer half-life, which is in agreement with theoretical predictions of 34.2 ns.
